name: Euphoric recall
statement: Euphoric recall is the clinical claim that people who use drugs remember the pleasure of past use and lose the memory of its costs.
meaning: The term belongs to addiction counselling rather than to experimental psychology. Its claim is that memories of intoxication keep their pleasant content while the harm attached to the same episodes drops away, and that the surviving half pulls a person back towards use. Vernon E. Johnson's 'I'll Quit Tomorrow' places it beside blackouts and repression, which frames it as a defence of the drinking rather than as an ordinary quirk of memory. The catalogue record for the 1980 revised edition lists a chapter titled 'Blackouts, repression, and euphoric recall'. The book's text could not be obtained, so nothing about its argument is stated here. In the journals the phrase travels as a mechanism taken for granted. A review of art therapy and addiction says that 'a major hurdle in addiction treatment is reducing the euphoric recall of substances during withdrawal cravings that lead to relapse'. An article proposing a compulsive eating phenotype writes that 'this "euphoric recall" persists and encourages overeating even after food loses its appeal'. Neither is a study of the thing named. No operational definition was located: no rating scale, no comparison condition, and no published measure.

origin.where: I'll Quit Tomorrow, revised edition, Harper & Row
origin.note: No source claiming to have coined the phrase was located. The earliest dated use found is the chapter title 'Blackouts, repression, and euphoric recall', which appears in the contents note of the catalogue record for the 1980 revised edition, 182 pages. Open Library records a first edition of 1973 at 168 pages, which was not checked, so the phrase may be older than the year given here. Both Internet Archive scans of the revised edition are lending restricted and returned HTTP 403 to the plain text and to the search-inside endpoint. HathiTrust full-text search returned 403 and the Google Books API was out of quota, so no earlier print use could be searched for in books.

evidence: No study measuring euphoric recall was located. The clinical sources make the claim by description and offer no ratings, no control condition and no comparison against what people said at the time. The nearest measured work sits one step away and asks a different question. Carter and Tiffany's meta-analysis of 41 cue-reactivity studies compared responses of alcoholics, cigarette smokers, cocaine addicts and heroin addicts to drug-related against neutral stimuli. Across all groups the effect size for self-reported craving was +0.92. Alcoholics gave a smaller craving effect size of +0.53 against +1.18 to +1.29 for the other groups, and the physiological effects were smaller: heart rate +0.26, sweat gland activity +0.40, skin temperature -0.24. Those figures are read from the abstract at Europe PMC, and they measure craving elicited by a cue, not the content of a remembered episode. The nearest theoretical treatment is Bornstein and Pickard's review in Neuropsychopharmacology, which proposes that drug choices are biased by selective sampling of individual episodic memories at the moment of decision. It is a framework paper reporting no new data, it takes its title from addiction folklore rather than from a measurement, and the phrase euphoric recall does not appear in its text as searched for this entry. Its own statement of the position is that despite evidence linking the hippocampus to addiction-related behaviours, 'the role of memory retrieval remains less well-understood, and potentially crucial'.

replication.headline: Nothing was found to replicate. Euphoric recall is a piece of clinical vocabulary with a long life in treatment settings and no experiment behind it that this search could find.
replication.detail: Europe PMC returns six records for the phrase, and all six use it in passing: a compulsive eating phenotype paper, an art therapy review, a philosophy of technology paper on personalised language models, a 2009 Mayo Clinic Proceedings letter on relapse in anaesthesia staff, a review of mirtazapine as pharmacotherapy, and a conference abstract book. A search of Europe PMC titles and abstracts for the phrase returns nothing. PubMed and NCBI Bookshelf both report the quoted phrase as not found in their indexes. Crossref returns no work whose title carries it and arXiv returns none. The APA Dictionary of Psychology has no entry for it. The nearest measured relatives are drug-cue reactivity and the fading affect bias, and both are different claims. Cue reactivity measures craving and arousal provoked by drug stimuli. The fading affect bias compares the emotion felt at an autobiographical event with the emotion felt on recalling it, across pleasant and unpleasant events, in general samples. Euphoric recall is a claim about what survives in the memory of a drug episode, made about dependent users. Treating the numbers from either literature as a measurement of it would be the error this entry warns about.

limits: The search covered Europe PMC by phrase and by title and abstract field, PubMed, NCBI Bookshelf, Crossref by title and by bibliographic query, arXiv, the Internet Archive item index, Open Library, and general web search. Four indexes went unsearched because they refused the request: OpenAlex for want of paid quota, Semantic Scholar with HTTP 429 on two attempts, the Google Books API for exceeded daily quota, and HathiTrust full-text search with HTTP 403. The Internet Archive full-text scrape endpoint failed with a 502 through the proxy and scholar.archive.org was rate limited. Only the English phrase was searched. None of the books that carry the concept was obtained: Johnson, and the works by Perkinson, Gorski, Keane, Washton and Zweben, and the Daley volume that the Wikipedia article cites. Three journal items named by that article were also not obtained, Hammersley's 1994 digest of memory phenomena in Addiction, Brown's 2000 paper in the Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, and Neighbors and colleagues on cognitive factors in addiction. So this entry cannot say who coined the phrase, when it first reached print, or whether any of those texts reports a measurement. An absence of evidence found by this search is not evidence that the clinicians are describing nothing.
misreadings: The first error is inherited from the lists. Euphoric recall sits in Wikipedia's catalogue of cognitive biases among entries that carry experiments, which invites a reader to expect an effect size, and none was located. The second is conflation with the measured memory effects nearby. Rosy retrospection compares evaluations of an event made before, during and after it. The fading affect bias compares the emotion at an event with the emotion at recall, and the finding is that unpleasant affect fades faster than pleasant affect. Euphoric recall is a claim about drug memories specifically, and about pleasant content being kept while harm is dropped, which is neither of those comparisons. The third is citation drift. Giubilini and four colleagues, writing in Science and Engineering Ethics, list 'the euphoric recall and negativity biases' and cite for both a chapter by Unkelbach, Alves and Koch whose title names negativity bias, positivity bias and valence asymmetries. That chapter was not obtained here, so this entry says only where the citation points. The last error is to read clinical currency as evidence. The phrase has been in treatment vocabulary since at least 1980 and is used in peer-reviewed articles as an accepted mechanism, and neither fact is a measurement.

sources.text: Internet Archive catalogue record for Johnson, V. E., I'll Quit Tomorrow, San Francisco: Harper & Row, 1980, 182 pages. Its contents note lists the chapter 'Blackouts, repression, and euphoric recall'. The scan is lending restricted and the text was not obtained; the same contents note appears on a second Internet Archive item for the same edition.
Open Library edition records for I'll Quit Tomorrow. Source for the first edition of 1973 at 168 pages, Harper & Row, and for the 1980 revised edition at 182 pages.

Carter, B. L., & Tiffany, S. T. (1999). Meta-analysis of cue-reactivity in addiction research. Addiction, 94(3), 327-340. The effect sizes quoted here are read from the structured abstract at Europe PMC; the full text was not obtained.

Bornstein, A. M., & Pickard, H. (2020). 'Chasing the first high': memory sampling in drug choice. Neuropsychopharmacology, 45(6), 907-915. Read in full as the Europe PMC rendered PDF. The nearest peer-reviewed treatment of the idea, and the source for the memory sampling framework described above.

Quinn, P. (2024). Art therapy's engagement of brain networks for enduring recovery from addiction. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 15, article 1458063. Europe PMC records the publication year as 2024 and Crossref dates it 6 January 2025. Read in full at Europe PMC. Quoted as an instance of the phrase used in a journal as a settled mechanism.

Tarman, V. I. (2025). Volume addiction: introducing a novel phenotype within compulsive high volume eating. Frontiers in Public Health, 13, article 1760037. Read in full at Europe PMC. Europe PMC records the publication year as 2025 and Crossref dates it 12 January 2026. Quoted as an instance of the phrase carried across to eating.

Giubilini, A., Porsdam Mann, S., Voinea, C., Earp, B., & Savulescu, J. (2024). Know thyself, improve thyself: personalized LLMs for self-knowledge and moral enhancement. Science and Engineering Ethics, 30(6), article 54. Read in full at Europe PMC. The source for the citation drift described above.

Unkelbach, C., Alves, H., & Koch, A. (2020). Negativity bias, positivity bias, and valence asymmetries: explaining the differential processing of positive and negative information. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 62, 115-187. Citation verified at Crossref. Not obtained; cited only as the work the preceding article points to.

Wikipedia, 'Euphoric recall', wikitext read on 10 August 2026. Used to find the books and papers named in the limits above, and cited as the object of the list problem described in misreadings, not as evidence for anything.
